u5c68f3e54c: When code calls a function that has not been declared, the warning ⟦1⟧warning: implicit declaration of function⟦/1⟧ appears. This warning means that you called a function without declaring it first.
uaa72bce3be: In some cases, this does affect the behavior of the program.
ud75cbc57ac: According to the C language standard, when a function has not been declared, its prototype is assumed to be as follows:
u993879089c: /* When foo has not been declared, its prototype is assumed to be as follows */
u0ea37b58f5: How to turn the warning into an error
u58929250d9: In general, you should declare a function's prototype before calling it, to avoid unexpected errors.
u34a15524d0: To make the compiler turn this warning into an error, add ⟦1⟧-Werror=implicit-function-declaration⟦/1⟧ to the compiler flags.
u1a314f85ef: Can floating-point numbers be used normally in C code?
u47a70d0419: Floating-point arithmetic can always be used in C code. The math library ⟦1⟧libm⟦/1⟧ (the library that contains functions such as ⟦2⟧tan⟦/2⟧ and ⟦3⟧sin⟦/3⟧) is also supported. The differences are as follows:
u47f9c96f59: Some chips have no ⟦1⟧hardware floating point⟦/1⟧ (that is, floating-point operations implemented by single hardware instructions). In this case, the compiler generates software implementations of the floating-point operations (that is, functions such as ⟦2⟧__adddf3⟦/2⟧ in the libcompiler_rt.a library).
u1cf81c39e7: Some chips support ⟦1⟧single-precision hardware floating point⟦/1⟧ (that is, single-precision ⟦2⟧float⟦/2⟧ operations are implemented by single hardware instructions). In this case, the compiler generates the corresponding instructions for single-precision operations, but double-precision floating-point operations are still implemented in software (for example, the double-precision floating-point addition ⟦3⟧__adddf3⟦/3⟧).
ubbadbf8e2e: The differences between hardware and software floating point lie mainly in computation speed and generated code size; the results are the same. Software implementations are slower and produce larger code.
ud3851c3a51: Which chips support single-precision hardware floating point?
u8a76a9c5d9: Currently, only some chips with the pi32v2 architecture support single-precision hardware floating point, namely the chips with the r3 or r4 version of the instruction set, that is, chips that are built with the ⟦1⟧-mcpu=r3⟦/1⟧ or ⟦2⟧-mcpu=r4⟦/2⟧ option.
u3d82644667: Why doesn't my code generate single-precision hardware floating-point instructions?
u1d2333a815: There are usually several possible causes
u3279ea098a: The current compiler options do not specify ⟦1⟧-mcpu=r3⟦/1⟧.
ud7964b47a6: For a library, check whether ⟦1⟧-mcpu=r3⟦/1⟧ was added when the library was built. (⟦2⟧Note that programmers may mistakenly set different -mcpu options for the library and the SDK⟦/2⟧. To get a library project whose settings match the SDK, see ⟦3⟧How to Get a Library Project from an Existing Standard SDK Project⟦/3⟧.)
u8504d8d008: The code itself does not use single-precision floating-point instructions.
u3ad413a862: Note that floating-point constants are ⟦1⟧double⟦/1⟧ by default. A constant is single precision only when f is appended to it. For example, ⟦2⟧1.0⟦/2⟧ is a ⟦3⟧double⟦/3⟧ and ⟦4⟧1.0f⟦/4⟧ is a ⟦5⟧float⟦/5⟧; only the latter is a single-precision floating-point number.
u184690c4db: When single-precision and double-precision values are mixed in an operation, the single-precision value is first promoted to double precision, and then a double-precision operation is performed.
ub5a3de3db1: Why does my code contain double-precision operations?
u0c8497e8d8: In general, we try to avoid double precision on chips that support only single-precision hardware floating point. In some cases, however, double-precision operations still appear; for example, you find calls to double-precision software functions such as ⟦1⟧__adddf3⟦/1⟧. The main reasons are as follows:
u71579eb207: Floating-point constants are ⟦1⟧double⟦/1⟧ by default. A constant is single precision only when f is appended to it. For example, ⟦2⟧1.0⟦/2⟧ is a ⟦3⟧double⟦/3⟧ and ⟦4⟧1.0f⟦/4⟧ is a ⟦5⟧float⟦/5⟧; only the latter is a single-precision floating-point number.
ub93161eb2b: When arguments are passed to a function with variable arguments (that is, ⟦1⟧...⟦/1⟧), they are promoted to double precision. For example, for a function such as ⟦2⟧int⟦/2⟧ ⟦3⟧printf(const char *fmt, ...)⟦/3⟧, when ⟦4⟧float a = 1.0f; printf("%f\n", a);⟦/4⟧ is executed, ⟦5⟧a⟦/5⟧ is promoted to ⟦6⟧double⟦/6⟧ before it is passed. Note that if a function has not been declared, its parameter list is assumed to be variable by default; see ⟦7⟧About Warnings for Calls to Undeclared Functions⟦/7⟧
u3970312512: Floating-point exceptions on the chip can be enabled or disabled. By default, the compiler assumes that floating-point exceptions are not enabled on the chip. That is, when a floating-point operation goes wrong, only a NaN is produced. For example, a division by zero gives NaN, but no exception occurs.
ub81eef708c: However, floating-point exceptions are sometimes enabled for debugging. In that case, errors such as division by zero cause an exception interrupt. To handle this, add ⟦1⟧-mllvm -floating-point-may-trap⟦/1⟧ to the compiler flags and ⟦2⟧--plugin-opt=-floating-point-may-trap⟦/2⟧ to the linker flags. These two options tell the compiler that floating-point operations may cause exceptions, so certain optimizations must not be performed.

u25d66d38d0: Check whether undeclared functions are being called; see ⟦1⟧About Warnings for Calls to Undeclared Functions⟦/1⟧

u0d27f5cd2f: When building on Linux or in WSL, ⟦1⟧ulimit -n 8096⟦/1⟧ was not run first to increase the number of files that can be opened, so the linker fails when the number of open files reaches the limit. (This problem is usually related to -flto mode combined with an .a file that contains a large number of .o files.
